# Editorial overview

## Problem-specific proof map

**A. Trie Prefix Count.** Incrementing every trie node visited by an inserted
word makes that node's count equal to the number of words sharing its prefix.
Following a query prefix therefore returns the desired count in its length.

**B. Palindrome Queries.** The local constraints permit direct mirrored
comparison: a substring is a palindrome exactly when every symmetric pair is
equal. This is `O(length)` per query and avoids probabilistic hash collisions.

**C. Distinct Substrings.** The local task uses a suffix automaton. State `v`
contributes `len[v]-len[link[v]]` distinct substring lengths, so summing these
over non-root states is linear in the number of automaton states. Enumeration
of all substrings is only a small-input stress-testing oracle.

## Detailed solution guide

**A. Trie Prefix Count.** Each trie node represents exactly one prefix: the
string on the path from the root to that node. During insertion, increment
`cnt` at the root and after moving to each next node. Therefore, after all
insertions, `cnt[v]` is the number of dictionary words whose path passes
through `v`, which is precisely the number of words with that prefix. A query
walks the prefix characters; a missing edge means zero matches.

**B. Palindrome Queries.** For the local constraints, comparing mirrored
characters is the clearest exact solution. For substring `[l,r]`, compare
`s[l]` with `s[r]`, then `s[l+1]` with `s[r-1]`, and so on. If all pairs match,
the substring equals its reverse. If one pair differs, the two strings differ at
a mirrored position, so it is not a palindrome. In a larger contest version,
the same condition can be checked with forward and reverse rolling hashes.

**C. Distinct Substrings.** The local solution is a suffix automaton. Each
state contributes `len[v] - len[link[v]]` new substrings: these are exactly the
lengths whose end-position class first appears at that state. Summing over
non-root states gives the answer. Enumerating every substring into a set is
correct only for tiny random tests used to validate the automaton.

**Common pitfalls.** Trie counters count prefixes, not terminal words only.
Palindrome queries must convert input indices consistently. For distinct
substrings, enumeration is pedagogical and exact at small limits, but a suffix
automaton is required for large external tasks.

This section shows three string representations.

- A uses a trie. Each inserted word increments counters on the nodes along its
  path, so the counter at the prefix endpoint is exactly the number of words
  with that prefix.
- B checks palindromes by comparing mirrored characters. For larger limits this
  can be replaced by forward/reverse hashes, but the local proof is exact.
- C counts distinct substrings with a suffix automaton. The local invariant is
  the contribution `len[v] - len[link[v]]` per non-root state; enumeration is
  reserved for tiny brute-force tests.

The editorial code uses the same asymptotically appropriate representation as
the local contract; brute force appears only as a testing oracle.

# A. Trie Prefix Count

## Restatement

Given dictionary words and prefix queries, count words having each prefix.

## Observations and algorithm

Each trie node is one prefix. Increment its counter for every inserted word
visiting it; walk a query to its endpoint and return that counter, or zero on a
missing edge. Inserting `apple, ape, bat` makes query `ap` return two.

## Correctness proof

After every insertion, a node counter equals the words with that node's prefix,
so the query endpoint is exactly the requested count. QED.

## Complexity

Work is linear in total inserted and queried characters; memory is one node per
distinct prefix.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std; struct Node{array<int,26> nx{}; int cnt=0;};
int main(){ios::sync_with_stdio(false);cin.tie(nullptr);int n,q;if(!(cin>>n>>q)) return 0; vector<Node> tr(1); for(int i=0;i<n;i++){string s;cin>>s;int v=0;tr[v].cnt++;for(char c:s){int x=c-'a';if(!tr[v].nx[x]){tr[v].nx[x]=tr.size();tr.push_back(Node());}v=tr[v].nx[x];tr[v].cnt++;}} while(q--){string p;cin>>p;int v=0;bool ok=true;for(char c:p){int x=c-'a';if(!tr[v].nx[x]){ok=false;break;}v=tr[v].nx[x];} cout<<(ok?tr[v].cnt:0)<<'\n';}}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys
def main():
    lines=sys.stdin.read().splitlines(); n,q=map(int,lines[0].split()); nxt=[]; cnt=[]
    nxt.append({}); cnt.append(0)
    for w in lines[1:1+n]:
        v=0; cnt[v]+=1
        for ch in w:
            if ch not in nxt[v]: nxt[v][ch]=len(nxt); nxt.append({}); cnt.append(0)
            v=nxt[v][ch]; cnt[v]+=1
    out=[]
    for p in lines[1+n:1+n+q]:
        v=0; ok=True
        for ch in p:
            if ch not in nxt[v]: ok=False; break
            v=nxt[v][ch]
        out.append(str(cnt[v] if ok else 0))
    print("\n".join(out))
if __name__=="__main__": main()
```

## Tests that matter

Test duplicate words, one word that prefixes another, an absent prefix, and a
one-character query.

# B. Palindrome Queries

## Restatement

For each substring query, print whether the substring is a palindrome.

## Observations and algorithm

The local bounds permit exact mirrored comparison. Convert inclusive 1-based
`[l,r]`, compare outward characters, and stop on a mismatch. In `abacaba`,
`[2,4]` is `bac` (NO) while `[3,5]` is `aca` (YES).

## Correctness proof

A substring equals its reverse iff each mirrored character pair is equal, which
is exactly the two-pointer condition. QED.

## Complexity

Each query is `O(r-l+1)` time and `O(1)` extra memory; this exact approach is
only suitable for the local small-query contract.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std; int main(){ios::sync_with_stdio(false);cin.tie(nullptr);string s;if(!(cin>>s)) return 0; int q;cin>>q; while(q--){int l,r;cin>>l>>r; string t=s.substr(l-1,r-l+1); string u=t; reverse(u.begin(),u.end()); cout<<(t==u?"YES":"NO")<<'\n';}}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys
def main():
    s=sys.stdin.readline().strip(); q=int(sys.stdin.readline()); out=[]
    for _ in range(q):
        l,r=map(int,sys.stdin.readline().split()); sub=s[l-1:r]; out.append("YES" if sub==sub[::-1] else "NO")
    print("\n".join(out))
if __name__=="__main__": main()
```

## Tests that matter

Test singleton, full string, even and odd lengths, and a mismatch in the outer
pair.

# C. Distinct Substrings

## Restatement

Print the number of distinct non-empty substrings of a string.

## Observations and algorithm

Build a suffix automaton. State v contributes `len[v]-len[link[v]]` new
substring lengths; sum this over non-root states. For `ababa`, the answer is 9.

## Correctness proof

Suffix links partition represented lengths into disjoint intervals, so every
distinct nonempty substring belongs to exactly one state's contribution. Clones
restore this invariant when a transition needs a shorter maximum length. QED.

## Complexity

There are at most `2*n-1` states. The fixed-alphabet version is `O(n)`; the
map-based listing is `O(n log alphabet)`.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std; struct St{map<char,int> nx; int link=-1,len=0;};
int main(){ios::sync_with_stdio(false);cin.tie(nullptr);string s;if(!(cin>>s)) return 0; vector<St> st(1); int last=0; for(char c:s){int cur=st.size();st.push_back(St());st[cur].len=st[last].len+1;int p=last;while(p!=-1&&!st[p].nx.count(c)){st[p].nx[c]=cur;p=st[p].link;} if(p==-1) st[cur].link=0; else {int q=st[p].nx[c]; if(st[p].len+1==st[q].len) st[cur].link=q; else {int clone=st.size();st.push_back(st[q]);st[clone].len=st[p].len+1;while(p!=-1&&st[p].nx[c]==q){st[p].nx[c]=clone;p=st[p].link;}st[q].link=st[cur].link=clone;}} last=cur;} long long ans=0; for(int v=1;v<(int)st.size();v++) ans+=st[v].len-st[st[v].link].len; cout<<ans<<'\n';}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys
def main():
    s=sys.stdin.readline().strip(); next=[]; link=[]; length=[]
    next.append({}); link.append(-1); length.append(0); last=0
    for ch in s:
        cur=len(next); next.append({}); length.append(length[last]+1); link.append(0); p=last
        while p!=-1 and ch not in next[p]: next[p][ch]=cur; p=link[p]
        if p==-1: link[cur]=0
        else:
            q=next[p][ch]
            if length[p]+1==length[q]: link[cur]=q
            else:
                clone=len(next); next.append(next[q].copy()); length.append(length[p]+1); link.append(link[q])
                while p!=-1 and next[p].get(ch)==q: next[p][ch]=clone; p=link[p]
                link[q]=link[cur]=clone
        last=cur
    print(sum(length[v]-length[link[v]] for v in range(1,len(next))))
if __name__=="__main__": main()
```

## Tests that matter

Test `a`, `aaa`, all distinct characters, and an alternating string.

# What to carry forward

Advanced algorithms become manageable when you state the invariant first, then code only the operations needed to preserve it.

# Complete upsolve notes

## A. Trie Prefix Count

Every node is one prefix and `count[node]` is the number of inserted words that
visit it. Insert `apple, ape, bat`: the node for `ap` has count two, while a
missing query edge returns zero immediately. Insert every word character by
character, incrementing the root and child after each move; walk each query and
return the endpoint count. The invariant follows by induction over inserted
words: exactly the words having a prefix pass through that node. Work is linear
in total inserted and queried characters, with one node per distinct prefix.
Use fixed 26-child arrays in C++ for lowercase input, dictionaries in Python for
clarity. Test duplicate words, one word that is a prefix of another, absent
queries, and a one-character query.

## B. Palindrome Queries

The local bounds permit exact two-pointer checking. Convert inclusive 1-based
`l,r` to zero-based positions, then compare outward characters while `l<r`.
For `abacaba`, `[2,4]` is `bac` and fails at `b,c`; `[3,5]` is `aca` and passes.
A substring equals its reverse iff every mirrored pair is equal, which proves
the test. A query costs `O(r-l+1)`, with `O(1)` extra memory; this is not the
right technique for very large query limits. C++ can use `substr` plus reverse
under the local contract, Python can use `s[l-1:r] == s[l-1:r][::-1]`. Test
singletons, full string, even and odd lengths, and a mismatch at the center's
outside pair.

## C. Distinct Substrings

The full listing uses a suffix automaton. After reading a prefix, `last` is the
state for that entire prefix; each state has maximum represented length `len`
and a suffix link to the largest proper suffix state. State v represents new
substring lengths `len[link[v]]+1..len[v]`, so its contribution is
`len[v]-len[link[v]]`. Summing non-root contributions counts every nonempty
distinct substring once. A clone copies transitions when the existing target
cannot have the required `len[p]+1`; redirecting suffix transitions restores
the state invariant. For `ababa`, the answer is nine. There are at most
`2*n-1` states and `O(n)` transitions for a fixed alphabet (the map-based local
listing is `O(n log alphabet)`). Test `a`, `aaa`, all distinct characters, and
an alternating string. Python dictionaries make the same construction viable.

# Testing discussion

Brute-force small trie prefixes by `word.startswith(prefix)`, palindrome
queries by reverse comparison, and distinct substrings with a set of all slices.

CP_TARGET=solution python3 sections/44_string_algorithms_ii/check.py
